name: Aaron Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm stockman and general hand at Kowalski's, which is a hundred and fifty beef cattle, eighty hectares of maize and grass, and a farm shop on the main road that sells our own beef. Mornings I do the feeding and check the herd, afternoons it's whatever's on, silage, fencing, loading cattle for the abattoir. I keep the herd records and work out the feed rations with an AI assistant on my phone, every day, and I set up the shop's online orders for Mrs Kowalski last spring.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the cattle and I like figuring things out, how to get a steer finished a month sooner on the same feed. What wears me out is working for someone else's profit when I can see how I'd run it. I live with my girlfriend Mia, she's a hairdresser in town, and we're saving to get engaged properly, but we've got less than a month put by. I want my own place one day, my own herd, like my grandfather had before he sold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hype. I'd be surprised, but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was oversold, but the people who used it sensibly still got ahead. I'd say that at the young farmers' club. I'm not one for complaining online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I keep my small edge. I'm faster with the records and the rations than anyone at Kowalski's, and that's worth something. If it all stalls, I'm still the only one on the farm who knows why the steers in pen four are doing better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the tools every day, and I'd keep pushing Mr Kowalski to let me run the shop's online side properly for a share of the extra sales. I'd keep saving for the ring. Nothing dramatic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit impatient, maybe, I like things moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What share of the shop sales would you ask for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five percent of anything above last year's online sales. It's not much, but it shows him I'm thinking like an owner. That's how my grandfather started, renting a field from a man who trusted him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think holds farms back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Red tape, mainly, and the big processors who set the price. If they let farmers sell direct and kept the forms short, a lad like me could build something. I don't want handouts, I want room.

S0.say: It was oversold, but people who used it sensibly still got ahead. He'd say that at the young farmers' club rather than online.
S0.think: He keeps his small edge with records and feed rations. He'd still be the one who understands why the cattle are doing well.
S0.do: Keeps using AI tools daily. Asks to run the farm shop's online sales for a five percent share of growth. Keeps saving for an engagement ring.
S0.feel: Calm and a bit impatient, since he likes things moving.
S0.quote: If it all stalls, I'm still the only one on the farm who knows why the steers in pen four are doing better.
S0.fieldNote: Aaron thinks like an owner already and frames everything around one day having his own herd, like his grandfather. He blames red tape and processors and wants room, not handouts. He uses AI daily as a business tool, not a toy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that one, I'd be ready for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say get on with it, the farms that adapt will win and the rest will sell to them. I'd say it at the young farmers' club and to Mr Kowalski. I wouldn't want the government picking winners, just keeping it fair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my chance. Robot feeders and fencing drones would cut the work on a cattle farm a lot, and someone has to run them. I'd rather be the man who owns two robots than the man who works next to one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn every machine I could get my hands on, the dealers run training days. I'd try to get a small loan to buy a second-hand robot feed pusher and rent it out to the smaller farms. I'd push Kowalski's to automate the feeding and let me run it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Excited, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got less than a month of savings. How would you pay for a robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A loan from the bank, or a deal with the dealer, pay as I go. It's a risk, I know. Mia would say I'm mad, and maybe I am, but my grandfather borrowed for his first tractor.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to the other workers at Kowalski's?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's only one other, Jan, and he's semi-retired. He'd probably finish a bit early. I'd feel for him, but it's how it goes.

S1.say: Get on with it, because farms that adapt will win. The government shouldn't pick winners, just keep it fair.
S1.think: This is his chance to own and run machines rather than work beside them. Robot feeders and fencing drones would cut farm work, and someone needs to run them.
S1.do: Learns machines through dealer training days. Takes a small loan or dealer deal to buy a second-hand robot feed pusher and rent it to smaller farms. Pushes his employer to automate feeding with him running it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be the man who owns two robots than the man who works next to one.
S1.fieldNote: Aaron would borrow with almost no savings, and he knows it's a risk. His grandfather's first tractor loan is his model. He's sympathetic but unsentimental about the semi-retired colleague who'd go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Hm. That's fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same, adapt or get left behind, but I'd be less sure saying it. I'd want the government to make sure small owners can buy the machines too, not just big companies. I'd say that to the farmers' union.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, two years is too fast for me to build anything. If anyone can buy a robot that does everything, the big outfits buy fifty and I buy one on credit, and they undercut me. I'd be twenty-nine, owing money on a robot that's out of date by Christmas.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't take the loan, not with two years. I'd cut spending, and Mia and I would hold off on the engagement party. I'd try to make money fast setting up systems for farms around here, and then look at what work there was, even if it meant moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not scared exactly, but tight in the stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Mia about the engagement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask her anyway, I've got the ring picked. But I'd say let's do the party later, at the farm shop, with a barbecue and our own beef. She'd say yes to that, I think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you lean on family or anyone else?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would help if he could, he's a builder. And our church has a men's group that helps people find work. I'd use that before anything from the government.

S2.say: Adapt or get left behind, he'd still say, though less confidently. The government should make sure small owners can buy machines too, not just big companies.
S2.think: Two years is too fast to build anything; big outfits would buy fleets and undercut him. He'd be left owing money on an outdated robot.
S2.do: Decides against taking a loan. Cuts spending and postpones the engagement party, though he'd still propose. Earns fast money setting up systems for local farms and would move for work if needed.
S2.feel: Anxious, tight in the stomach rather than scared.
S2.quote: I'd be twenty-nine, owing money on a robot that's out of date by Christmas.
S2.fieldNote: Aaron's appetite for risk turns sensible here: he drops the loan plan immediately. He'd still propose but delay the party, which is very him. He'd turn to his father and church before the state.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay. That's tight, but it's a window.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the next five years are for people who move first. I'd tell the young farmers' club to stop waiting and start learning. I'd want the government to keep the rules simple so small operators can compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think five years gives me two or three good years to build a small contracting business, running robots for farms that don't want to own them. Then it's a question of whether I can stay ahead of the big firms. It's a gamble, but I'd rather gamble than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start this winter, setting up feeding and records systems for neighbours, paid by the job. In year two, if it was going well, I'd take a small loan for one machine. I'd save what I could, and keep the job at Kowalski's until the side business paid more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More excited than not, but I'd know the clock was running.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop and pull back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If I couldn't keep the machine busy three days a week. That's my line. My grandfather said never buy a tractor you can't keep busy, and a robot's the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years change, compared with the two-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They change whether I borrow. In two years, no chance. In five, I'd borrow once the business had shown it could pay, and that makes all the difference.

S3.say: The next five years are for people who move first, so stop waiting and start learning. Rules should stay simple so small operators can compete.
S3.think: Five years gives him two or three good years to build a robot contracting business before the big firms catch up. It's a gamble he'd prefer to waiting.
S3.do: Starts setting up feeding and record systems for neighbours this winter. Takes a small loan for one machine in year two if the business is working. Keeps his farm job until the side business earns more.
S3.feel: Uneasy, more excited than worried, but aware the clock is running.
S3.quote: My grandfather said never buy a tractor you can't keep busy, and a robot's the same.
S3.fieldNote: The extra time decides whether Aaron borrows, and he sets himself a clear rule for pulling back. His grandfather's advice keeps coming back. He is clear-eyed about competition from big firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. That's enough to build something real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best chance in a generation for young people to own their own farm business again. I'd want fewer rules and fair access to finance for small operators. I'd say that loudly at the young farmers' club.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think ten years is long enough to go from farmhand to owner. I'd build a contracting business with robots, and maybe rent land in a few years and run my own herd with machines doing the heavy work. My grandfather sold his herd because he couldn't afford the help, and the robots might be what lets me buy one back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the side business this winter and save from it. In year two or three I'd buy my first machine with a loan, and add one a year if they paid. By year five I'd look for a small rented farm, maybe forty hectares, and run cattle on it with robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Honestly, I'd be excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you worry about, even with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the big companies buy up all the land before I can rent any. That's the real risk. Robots I can afford, land I might never.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do Mia and your plans for a family fit into that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd get married in the next year or two, and children a few years after, once the business was paying. Mia would keep her salon chair in town, people will want a person to cut their hair for a long time, I reckon.

S4.say: This is the best chance in a generation for young people to own farm businesses again. Small operators need fewer rules and fair access to finance.
S4.think: Ten years is long enough to go from farmhand to owner, first with a robot contracting business and later a small rented herd. Robots might let him buy back what his grandfather sold.
S4.do: Starts the side business this winter and saves from it. Buys a first machine on a loan in year two or three, adding one a year if they pay. Looks to rent a forty-hectare farm by year five and run cattle with robots.
S4.feel: Calm and excited, with a worry about big companies buying up land.
S4.quote: Robots I can afford, land I might never.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Aaron sees robots as the help his grandfather couldn't afford. His worry moves from machines to land, which he thinks will be harder to get than robots. His marriage and family plans fit around the business timeline.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. No time to build anything, and the big firms buy fifty robots while I'm still deciding on one. What would help is fair loans for young farmers to buy machines, and land kept available to rent, not all bought up by the big companies.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about who owns things. Everyone asks about jobs, but if I owned a few robots I wouldn't need a job. I'd want young people to have a fair shot at owning, not just working.

headlineQuote: My grandfather sold his herd because he couldn't afford the help, and the robots might be what lets me buy one back.
portrait: Aaron Ziegler is a 27-year-old stockman on a 150-head beef farm with a roadside farm shop, living with his hairdresser girlfriend Mia and saving for an engagement with less than a month in the bank. He uses AI daily for herd records and feed rations and dreams of buying back the herd his grandfather sold. Traditional and pro-market, he wants room and fair finance, not handouts. He's calm at a plateau and excited by steady change, anxious at AGI in two years when he'd drop any loan plans, and increasingly upbeat with five or ten years, planning a robot contracting business and eventually his own rented farm.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because there'd be no time to build a business before big firms bought robots by the fleet.
whatWouldHelp: Fair loans for young farmers to buy machines, and land kept available to rent rather than bought up by big companies.
